criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1. The article examines an acute E. coli contamination outbreak in an existing municipal piped drinking-water system in Walkerton, Ontario, and how discourses of science, law, and nationalism in the subsequent Public Inquiry constituted resistance to neo-liberalism. Per the scope discipline rules, drinking-water quality/contamination is not interchangeable with household or community water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2, but FAILS the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain broad wording, the paper examines legal, regulatory, and governance factors including Ontario Ministry of the Environment (MoE) budget and staff cuts, privatization of water-testing laboratories in 1996, treating adverse test notification as a non-binding guideline rather than law, grandfathering of older wells under the 1994 Ontario Drinking Water Objectives, non-enforcement (failure to issue a Director's Order), and the legal/evidentiary procedures of the Walkerton Public Inquiry. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, however, none of these mechanisms govern household or community water or sanitation service access (eligibility, tenure/documentation, tariffs/affordability, connection, or disconnection); they concern drinking-water quality safety regulation and macro-political/discursive resistance to neo-liberal governance.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative socio-legal case study and discourse analysis drawing on primary documentary sources from the Walkerton Public Inquiry, including verbatim hearing transcripts (114 witnesses, subpoenaed MoE records/exhibits), newspaper coverage, and the O'Connor Report (2002).
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4. Reported outcomes are waterborne morbidity and mortality from E. coli O157:H7 contamination (7 deaths and 2,321 illnesses) and political/discursive and legislative shifts following the O'Connor Report (e.g., enactment of the Safe Drinking Water Act 2002), rather than household or community water or sanitation access, connection, availability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion. (A May-to-December Boil Water Advisory is mentioned only in passing as chronology.)
criterion_notes.c5: The case context and units of analysis (the Walkerton Public Inquiry, Ontario's MoE regulatory regime, and the town of Walkerton, Ontario, population 4,800), regulatory/discursive exposures, health and policy outcomes, and qualitative socio-legal case-study design are identifiable from the full text.

evidence_quotes.quote: when seven people died and 2300 became ill after E. Coli contaminated public drinking water in May of 2000.
The Inquiry was to look into the contamination of the water supply in Walkerton and the safety of Ontario’s drinking water. From 20 October 2000 to 8 August 2001, 114 witnesses were heard.

Out of a myriad of causes – from incompetence to climate – the Report singles out government cutbacks and neo-liberal policies. Each policy failure merits a separate chapter: the targeting of the MoE by the Red Tape Commission, the anti-regulatory philosophy, the disincentives to regulation.
The primary source for this section is the Walkerton Report (O’Connor, 2002: 1–38), supplemented by newspaper reports and witness testimony at the Public Inquiry.
In all 2321 people became ill: 1346 were treated, 65 hospitalized, and 27 developed Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS), a serious complication.

raw_response.exposure: Neo-liberal deregulation in Ontario (MoE budget and staff cuts, privatization of water-testing laboratories without mandatory adverse-result reporting laws, non-enforcement of water-quality inspections) and legal/scientific discourses mobilized in the Walkerton Public Inquiry
raw_response.outcome: Acute E. coli drinking-water contamination outbreak (7 deaths and 2,321 illnesses) and discursive/legislative resistance to neo-liberalism culminating in the O'Connor Report and Ontario's Safe Drinking Water Act (2002)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Case study of the Walkerton Public Inquiry (114 witnesses, including 31 scientists, and over 3,000 documentary exhibits) concerning the May 2000 municipal water contamination disaster in Walkerton, Ontario (town population 4,800)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; also fails Criterion 4 on access outcomes and narrow Criterion 2). Snider (2004) presents a qualitative socio-legal case study of the May 2000 E. coli drinking-water contamination disaster in Walkerton, Ontario, and analyzes how discourses of law, science, and Canadian nationalism in the Walkerton Public Inquiry (O'Connor Report) challenged neo-liberal deregulation. While the paper examines regulatory and governance factors under the plain wording of Criterion 2 (laboratory privatization, non-binding reporting guidelines, MoE budget/inspection cuts, and non-enforcement), those rules govern drinking-water quality/safety rather than household or community service access, and the paper reports health/contamination and discursive/legislative outcomes rather than water or sanitation service access outcomes. Therefore, it is excluded under both the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 reading and the plain Criterion 2 wording.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative socio-legal case study and discourse analysis of Public Inquiry transcripts, documentary exhibits, media reports, and the O'Connor Report
